name: Fundamentals-adjusted currency value (Menkhoff et al. 2017)

how_it_works.simple: Some currencies get cheap compared to what they can buy. But some are cheap for a good reason, like a country getting poorer. This strategy buys currencies that are cheap for no good reason and sells ones that are pricey for no good reason.
how_it_works.analogy: Like shopping for a used car: a low price only counts as a bargain after you account for the mileage and condition.
how_it_works.precise: Take each currency's 5-year change in the real exchange rate against the USD as the raw value signal. Each quarter, regress that signal cross-sectionally on (expected) productivity, export quality, net foreign assets over GDP and the output gap. The residual is the adjusted value signal; sort currencies on it and go long undervalued, short overvalued.

rule: Each quarter, compute the 5-year log real exchange rate change for each currency versus USD, regress it across countries on real GDP per capita, export quality, NFA/GDP and output gap (or their EWMA or VAR forecasts), and hold rank-weighted long positions in currencies with the most positive residual (cheapest) and short positions in those with the most negative residual, rebalanced quarterly.
data_needed: Spot exchange rates vs USD, quarterly (end of quarter)
CPI by country (to build real exchange rates)
Forward rates or short-term interest rates for excess returns
Real GDP per capita, output gap, net foreign assets/GDP (Lane and Milesi-Ferretti), IMF export quality index
economic_rationale: Real exchange rates tend to revert, but part of a currency's real move reflects fundamentals that do not mean revert; stripping those out leaves a cleaner measure of the currency risk premium (Menkhoff, Sarno, Schmeling and Schrimpf 2017).
why_it_might_fail: Macro inputs are low frequency, revised and partly unavailable in real time (the paper notes export quality data cover a short window), so live signals may be noisier than the backtest. Hutchinson et al. (2022) find currency value predictability disappeared after publication of the evidence.

reported_results.source: Menkhoff et al. 2017, Table 4 (CEPR working paper version)
reported_results.market: 22 currencies vs USD (23 advanced and emerging economies)
reported_results.notes: Benchmark (unadjusted) value: rank portfolio sorted on 5-year real exchange rate change. HML of 4 bins had Sharpe 0.44, mean 3.89%, vol 8.93%. No transaction costs mentioned.

reported_results.source: Menkhoff et al. 2017, Table 5 Panel D (CEPR working paper version)
reported_results.notes: Adjusted value: rank portfolio on residual after regressing on panel-VAR expected fundamentals. Linear-weight version: Sharpe 0.91, mean 2.43%, vol 2.68%. Gain comes from lower volatility, not higher mean. Expected fundamentals are estimated recursively, but regressions use the cross-section at each date.

post_publication_evidence: Hutchinson, Kyziropoulos, O'Brien, O'Reilly and Sharma (2022, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.irfa.2022.102245; abstract at https://zenodo.org/records/7326532) replicated published currency carry, momentum and value studies and found the average out-of-sample Sharpe ratio fell from +0.39 before publication to -0.32 after it, with currencies no longer responding to interest rate and real exchange rate differentials. AQR's century study (Ilmanen et al., 2021) reports a currency value Sharpe ratio of 0.69 after publication against 0.72 in the original sample, the best post-publication record of any currency style it tests (carry: -0.17). The BIS publishes free monthly real effective exchange rates for emerging markets, so a simplified EM version is testable (RES-0014).

relevance.reason: A slow, low-turnover FX signal that diversifies carry and momentum, but it needs macro data that is hard to assemble point in time for free.

research.notes: RES-0014 ranks an EM version second among candidates.
